explanations.explanation: Right on the money, baker. The very first verse says, "This is the account of Esau (that is, Edom)." (Genesis 36:1) Two names, one man. Verse 8 says it again, and verse 43 ends by calling Esau "the father of the Edomites." That's a name with a whole nation hanging off it.

Close, and it's an easy mix-up, because "Israel" is a name in this family. But it belongs to Esau's brother Jacob, not to Esau (Genesis 32:28). Genesis 36:1 says, "This is the account of Esau (that is, Edom)." So the answer is Edom. Two brothers, two names, and I'd keep a sticky note handy.

Ephraim is a name from the family too, but it isn't Esau's. Ephraim is one of Joseph's sons (Genesis 41:52). The verse here says, "This is the account of Esau (that is, Edom)." (Genesis 36:1) So Edom is the other name for Esau. Plenty of names in this chapter, friend, so no shame in a mix-up.

That's the one. Verse 3 says Basemath is the "daughter of Ishmael and sister of Nebaioth." (Genesis 36:3) Ishmael was Abraham's son (Genesis 25:12). So Esau's wife comes from Abraham's family, too. Notice the text names her brother, Nebaioth, as well.

Laban was Jacob's father-in-law (Genesis 29:16-23), so I see why he came to mind. But he's not Basemath's father. Verse 3 says she is the "daughter of Ishmael and sister of Nebaioth." (Genesis 36:3) Laban has plenty to do in Jacob's story already. He doesn't need to be in Esau's too.

Lot was Abraham's nephew (Genesis 12:5), so he's in the family story somewhere, just not here. Basemath is the "daughter of Ishmael and sister of Nebaioth." (Genesis 36:3) Ishmael is the answer. Lots of L's in this family, friend. I'm already squinting at the page myself.

Yes, baker. Verse 5 says these were the sons of Esau, "who were born to him in the land of Canaan." (Genesis 36:5) All five of them, Eliphaz, Reuel, Jeush, Jalam and Korah, were born there before the big move. The family tree starts in Canaan and grows from there.

Paddan-aram is where Jacob lived for years with Laban, and where his sons were born (Genesis 28:2; 29:32). That's Jacob's story, though. Esau's sons were "born to him in the land of Canaan." (Genesis 36:5) Easy to cross the wires with two brothers and two sets of kids.

Egypt does show up later in Genesis, but not for these five boys. Verse 5 says they "were born to him in the land of Canaan." (Genesis 36:5) So Canaan is the answer. Egypt is a long walk from Esau's tent, friend, and I wouldn't try it with a cookie box in my mustache.

Not quite, baker. Verse 6 says Esau took "his livestock, all his other animals, and all the property he had acquired in Canaan." (Genesis 36:6) Nothing got left behind. If I read that right, he took the whole herd with him. That's a lot of animals to count at the door.

False is right. Verse 6 says Esau took "his livestock, all his other animals, and all the property he had acquired in Canaan." (Genesis 36:6) He didn't leave the herd behind. Verse 7 adds that their possessions were too great for them to dwell together. So the livestock went right along with him.

True. Verse 6 says Esau moved "to a land far away from his brother Jacob." (Genesis 36:6) Then verse 8 says he settled in the area of Mount Seir. The text tells us where he went and how big the move was. It doesn't say anything more about how the brothers felt.

Not this time, friend. Verse 6 says Esau "moved to a land far away from his brother Jacob." (Genesis 36:6) So the move was a far one, not around the corner. He ended up in the area of Mount Seir (Genesis 36:8).

explanations.answer: They own too much for the land to support
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives. Verse 7 says, "For their possessions were too great for them to dwell together; the land where they stayed could not support them because of their livestock." (Genesis 36:7) Too many animals, not enough land. I've had a kitchen like that. Too many cookies, not enough counter.

explanations.answer: They have another fight over a blessing
explanations.explanation: The two brothers did have a fight over a blessing earlier (Genesis 27:36). But that's not the reason given here. Verse 7 says, "For their possessions were too great for them to dwell together; the land where they stayed could not support them because of their livestock." (Genesis 36:7) This move comes down to stuff and space.

explanations.answer: God tells Esau to leave the land of Canaan
explanations.explanation: This passage doesn't say that. Genesis 36 never mentions God telling Esau to go anywhere. The reason it gives is in verse 7: "For their possessions were too great for them to dwell together; the land where they stayed could not support them because of their livestock." (Genesis 36:7) We stick with what the text says, baker.

explanations.answer: In the area of Mount Seir
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Verse 8 says, "So Esau (that is, Edom) settled in the area of Mount Seir." (Genesis 36:8) Verse 9 repeats it and calls him "the father of the Edomites." The Horites, Seir's sons, were already living in that land (Genesis 36:20).

explanations.answer: In the area of Mount Carmel
explanations.explanation: Mount Carmel is a real mountain in the Bible. Elijah, the prophet, has a showdown there in 1 Kings 18:19-20. But Esau didn't settle there. Verse 8 says, "So Esau (that is, Edom) settled in the area of Mount Seir." (Genesis 36:8) Wrong mountain, friend, but good mountain.

explanations.answer: In the area of Mount Sinai
explanations.explanation: Mount Sinai matters a lot later in the Bible, because God gives the law there (Exodus 19:20). But it's not where Esau settled. Verse 8 says, "So Esau (that is, Edom) settled in the area of Mount Seir." (Genesis 36:8) Sinai and Seir both start with S. That's about as far as the match goes.
